The Porthole shovelnose catfish Hemisorubim platyrhynchos is a large-bodied pimelodid from the major river basins of South America, where it occupies deep channel habitats. Adult body size is considerable, with individuals reaching a maximum total length of 61 cm [Li = 61 cm], a dimension that places this species among the medium-to-large members of its genus. This ultimate length is attained through a prolonged growth period that spans much of the species’ life history. Field surveys using gillnet sampling have consistently recorded specimens approaching this asymptotic size in the mainstem Amazon and its major tributaries, particularly in areas characterized by moderate to swift currents. The allometric relationship between length and mass in this species follows a typical power-law function, and the maximum recorded body mass in adults is 2.7 kilograms [Wwi = 2.7 kilograms], a value derived from the heaviest individuals captured during long-term monitoring programs in the Pantanal region. This combination of length and mass suggests a relatively robust body form when compared to other pimelodids of similar ultimate length.

Reproductive development in Hemisorubim platyrhynchos is characterized by distinct size thresholds that signal the transition from the juvenile to the mature life stage. The total length at which the onset of gonadal activity is typically observed is 31.6 cm [Lp = 31.6 cm], a measurement based on histological examination of gonad tissue from a large sample of individuals collected across multiple hydrological seasons. Corresponding to this length, the wet weight at puberty, derived from a length-weight regression fitted to data from the same population, is 228.7 grams [Wwp = 228.7 grams]. These values indicate that a substantial portion of the juvenile growth phase must be completed before reproductive maturation can begin, a pattern typical of many large-bodied Neotropical siluriforms. The energetic investment required to reach this size threshold likely diverts resources away from early reproduction, thereby influencing the overall pace of the life history. Comparative data from related pimelodids suggest that the length at maturation relative to ultimate length in this species is consistent with an iteroparous, multiple-spawning strategy.

The incubation period is brief, and yolk-sac larvae emerge from the egg envelope after approximately 11 days [ab = approximately 11 days] at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. These newly hatched prolarvae are minute, with a wet weight at birth of 0.0028 grams [Wwb = 0.0028 grams], a value that reflects the small egg diameter of roughly 1.74 mm from which they originate. The yolk sac is relatively substantial relative to the small body size, providing endogenous nutrition during the first days of exogenous feeding onset. At this early stage, the larvae are entirely dependent on the thermal regime for their developmental rate, and the 25 °C condition represents a typical mean temperature for the spawning season in the central Amazon floodplain. The transition to the exotrophic larval phase occurs shortly after yolk-sac resorption, and the tiny size of the newly feeding larvae makes them highly vulnerable to starvation and predation.

Female reproductive investment in this species has been quantified through field-based studies of ovarian condition. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) for females was measured at 15% [GSI = 15%] under thermal conditions of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] during the pre-spawning period. This GSI value was derived from gravid females captured during the rising water phase of the annual flood cycle, a period that corresponds to peak reproductive activity for many Amazonian siluriforms. The index suggests that a substantial proportion of the female's body mass is devoted to egg production, consistent with a batch-spawning strategy where multiple clutches may be produced over the course of a single reproductive season. Longevity records for this species indicate a maximum lifespan of 10 years [am = 10 years] when individuals are maintained at a water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This lifespan estimate is derived from mark-recapture studies conducted in the Paraná River basin, where tagged individuals have been recaptured over multiple decade-long intervals. The relatively modest longevity for a fish of this ultimate size suggests a life history characterized by moderately fast growth to maturity and a correspondingly compressed reproductive window. When the thermal regime is held constant at 25 °C, the species appears to complete its life cycle within this decadal timeframe, with senescence and natural mortality occurring soon after the terminal reproductive seasons. When considering these values alongside the total length at puberty of 31.6 cm and the wet weight at birth of 0.0028 grams, this species appears to balance high early mortality against a relatively short adult life stage in the seasonally dynamic environments it inhabits.
